cw/agentless@2/bash.description: Run a shell command in the working directory and return its combined stdout and stderr as one text; there is no separate exit code field, so print it yourself (for example `; echo "exit=$?"`) when it matters. Each call starts a fresh shell; chain commands with && or cd inside the command. Commands must be non-interactive. `stage` labels the call as part of LOCALIZE, REPAIR or VALIDATE; it is recorded and does not change how the command runs. Prefer `grep`, `glob` and `read` for searching and viewing files.

timeout.description: Optional. Time limit in milliseconds before the command is killed.

cw/agentless@2/read.description: Show a file with each line numbered as `N: text`, starting at 1 (up to 2000 lines unless `num_lines` is set; the output says where to continue), or list the entries of a directory. Use `line_start` and `num_lines` to view one region of a large file. Read the exact region you plan to change right before calling `edit`. For binary or very large files, `bash` with `head -c`, `od` or `strings` is often better.

path.description: Absolute path of the file or directory.

num_lines.description: Optional. How many lines to show.

cw/agentless@2/glob.description: Find files whose names match a glob pattern such as "**/*.py" or "**/CMakeLists.txt". The pattern is relative to the search directory; a bare "*.py" matches only the top level, so start with "**/" to search at any depth. Returns matching paths, most recently modified first. Use it to map the structure at the file level of localization.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match file names against.

path.description: Optional. Directory to search in; defaults to the working directory.

cw/agentless@2/grep.description: Search file contents with a regular expression and return the matching lines, each with its file path and line number. Use it for every concrete clue in the task: identifiers, error messages, option names. Narrow the search with `path` and `file_filter`.

path.description: Optional. Directory to search in; defaults to the working directory.

file_filter.description: Optional. Glob limiting which files are searched, for example "*.py" or "*.{c,h}".

cw/agentless@2/edit.description: Apply one search/replace block to an existing file that you have already opened with `read` (a file that changed on disk since then must be read again): the text `old_text` is replaced with `new_text`. `old_text` must match the file exactly, whitespace and indentation included, and must occur exactly once; add surrounding lines if it is not unique. The call fails if there is no match or more than one. Keep each block to the localized lines.

path.description: Absolute path of the file to change.

old_text.description: Exact text to find; must occur once.

cw/agentless@2/write.description: Create a file, or replace a file's whole content, with `content`. Parent directories are created. To replace an existing file, `read` it first; otherwise the call is refused. Use it for new files such as a reproduction script or a missing configuration file; use `edit` for changes to existing code.

path.description: Absolute path of the file to write.

cw/aider@2/edit.description: Apply one SEARCH/REPLACE edit to an existing file. `search` is the SEARCH section: a contiguous chunk of the file, copied exactly (comments, docstrings, whitespace and indentation included). It must occur exactly once in the file; add surrounding lines until it is unique. `replace` is the REPLACE section that takes its place; give an empty string to delete the lines. If `search` is not found, or is found more than once, nothing is changed and an error is returned. Keep edits small: the changing lines plus a few lines of context. The file must have been read with `read` first; an edit to a file you have not read, or that changed on disk since, is refused. `search` must not be empty; create new files with `write`.

path.description: Path of the file to edit, verbatim, relative to the working directory or absolute.

search.description: SEARCH section: the exact existing lines to find (not empty). Must match once.

replace.description: REPLACE section: the lines to put in place of the SEARCH section.

cw/aider@2/read.description: Show the contents of a file, each line numbered as `N: text`, so you can copy exact SEARCH text for `edit`. The line numbers are not part of the file. Given a folder `path`, it lists the folder's entries instead. For long files, give `first_line` (1-based) and `max_lines` to see one part at a time; without them it shows up to 2000 lines and says where to continue.

path.description: Path of the file or folder to show.

first_line.description: Optional. Line number to start at, counting from 1.

max_lines.description: Optional. How many lines to show.

cw/aider@2/bash.description: Run a shell command in the working directory and return what it printed, with stdout and stderr combined in one text (there is no separate exit-code field; append `; echo "exit=$?"` when you need it). Use it to run tests, builds and scripts, to look around (ls, find, git status), and to rename or delete files. Commands cannot be interactive; do not depend on network access. `timeout_ms` is optional; set it for long test suites or builds.

shell_cmd.description: The shell command line to run.

timeout_ms.description: Optional. Maximum run time in milliseconds.

cw/aider@2/grep.description: Search the contents of files for a regular expression and return the matching lines, each with its file path and line number. Use it to find where a function, class, setting or error message lives before you read and edit. `path` limits the search to one folder (default: the working directory); `file_glob` limits it to file names such as "*.py" or "*.{ts,tsx}".

regex.description: The regular expression to search for.

path.description: Optional. Folder to search in.

file_glob.description: Optional. Only search files whose names match this pattern.

cw/amazonq@1/bash.description:
Runs a bash command in the sandbox and returns its stdout and stderr combined into one output. No separate exit code is reported; append `; echo "exit=$?"` to the command when you need it. After a pipeline, `$?` is the last command's status; prefix `set -o pipefail;` when you pipe into head or tail. A command that runs past its time limit is killed and the output says so.

Guidelines:
- Commands must be non-interactive; never start an editor, pager or prompt that waits for input.
- Run servers and other long-lived processes in the background, with output redirected to a log file.
- Avoid commands that print huge amounts of output; filter or truncate them.
- Use `cwd` to choose a directory instead of prefixing the command with cd.
- `timeout_ms` caps how long the command may run; slow builds may need a larger value.
- Do not run destructive commands outside the working directory, and do not rewrite git history. The sandbox refuses rm -rf on absolute paths and git network or history-mining commands (fetch, pull, clone, log --all, reflog); delete with relative paths.

summary.description: A brief explanation of what the command does and why it is being run.

cwd.description: Optional absolute directory to run the command in. Defaults to the working directory.

cw/amazonq@1/read.description:
Reads a text file or lists a directory.

Modes:
- "Line": returns the lines of the file at `path`, numbered. Each line is shown as `N: text`. Without `start_line` and `max_lines`, it reads from the top up to 2000 lines and ends with a hint naming the `start_line` to continue from. Set `start_line` (1-based) and `max_lines` to read one region of a large file.
- "Directory": lists the entries of the directory at `path`. Leave `start_line` and `max_lines` unset.

`path` must be absolute. Read a file before changing it: edit and write refuse to modify an existing file that has not been read first, and `old_str` in edit should be copied from the real text.

mode.description: Line to read a file, Directory to list a directory.

path.description: Absolute path to the file or directory.

start_line.description: Optional. First line to return, 1-based. Line mode only.

max_lines.description: Optional. Number of lines to return. Line mode only.

summary.description: Optional. Why this read is needed.

cw/amazonq@1/write.description:
Creates a file, or overwrites an existing one, with `file_text`. Missing parent directories are created.

- `file_text` is the complete content of the file; anything not in it is gone after the call.
- An existing file must be read with read before it can be overwritten; otherwise the call is refused.
- For a small change to an existing file, use edit instead.

path.description: Absolute path of the file to create or overwrite.

summary.description: One sentence describing what this file is for or what changed.

cw/amazonq@1/edit.description:
Replaces one occurrence of `old_str` with `new_str` in the file at `path`.

- `old_str` must match the file exactly, whitespace and indentation included, and must occur exactly once. If it occurs more than once, include more surrounding lines so it becomes unique.
- `new_str` is the replacement text; use an empty string to delete `old_str`.
- To add text, pick a unique nearby line as `old_str` and repeat it in `new_str` together with the new lines.
- The file must have been read with read first; otherwise the call is refused.
- To change several places, make one call per place.

path.description: Absolute path of the file to change.

old_str.description: Exact text to replace; must occur exactly once.

new_str.description: Text to put in its place.

cw/amazonq@1/grep.description: Searches file contents for lines matching a regular expression `pattern` and returns each matching line with its file path and line number. Narrow the search with `path` (a directory) and `file_pattern` (a glob such as "*.ts"). Use it to find definitions, call sites, error messages and config keys.

path.description: Optional absolute directory to search in.

file_pattern.description: Optional glob that limits which files are searched.

cw/amp@2/bash.description:
Executes the given shell command in the user's default shell.

## Important notes

1. Directory verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use the read tool to check that the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
   - For example, before running a command that writes into `build/out`, read the `build` directory.

2. Working directory:
   - If `cwd` is not given, the command runs in the workspace root.
   - Each call runs in a new shell, so `cd` does not carry over between calls. Pass an absolute `cwd` instead of prefixing the command with `cd`.

3. Multiple independent commands:
   - Do NOT chain unrelated commands with `;`.
   - Use `&&` only when a later command depends on an earlier one succeeding.
   - Commands that do not depend on each other can be issued as separate bash calls in the same response.

4. Output:
   - Standard output and standard error are returned together as one text when the command finishes. There is no separate exit code; add `; echo "exit=$?"` to `cmd` when you need it. After a pipeline, `$?` is the last command's status, so prefix `set -o pipefail;` when you pipe into `head` or `tail`.
   - Very long output is truncated, so filter it with `head`, `tail` or `grep` when you expect a lot.
   - A command that runs for more than about two minutes is killed, and the output says so. Start longer jobs in the background with output sent to a log file, and check the log in later calls.

5. Never run commands that wait for input or never exit (editors, pagers, REPLs, foreground servers). Pass non-interactive flags such as `--yes`, and start long-running servers in the background with their output redirected to a log file.

6. Do not use this tool to read files, list directories or search; use read, glob and grep. For a binary or very large file, `head -c`, `od` or `strings` is fine.

7. Outside network access is not guaranteed; do not depend on it. The sandbox refuses `rm -rf` on absolute paths (use relative paths) and git fetch, pull, clone, `git log --all` and `git reflog`. Use it for builds, tests, package managers, version control and other shell work.

## Examples

- To run the tests of one package: `cmd` = `go test ./internal/cache/...`, `cwd` = the repository root
- To install dependencies: `cmd` = `npm ci`, `cwd` = the directory holding package.json

cwd.description: Absolute path to a directory where the command will be executed (must be absolute, not relative). Defaults to the workspace root.

cw/amp@2/read.description:
Read a file from the file system. If the path is a directory, it returns a list of the entries in it instead.

- The `path` parameter MUST be an absolute path.
- By default this tool returns the first 2000 lines. To see more of a large file, pass `offset` (the 1-based line number to start at) and `limit` (how many lines to return).
- The contents are returned with each line prefixed by its line number (`N: text`); when more lines remain, the output ends with a hint giving the `offset` to continue from. When you copy text into edit, leave the line-number prefix out.
- When you need several files, read them all in the same response.
- Do not read a file again right after editing it to check the edit; edit reports an error if the change could not be made.

path.description: The absolute path to the file or directory (MUST be absolute, not relative).

offset.description: Optional 1-based line number to start reading from.

limit.description: Optional maximum number of lines to return.

cw/amp@2/edit.description:
Make edits to a text file.

Replaces `old_str` with `new_str` in the given file.

Returns a short confirmation of the change.

The file specified by `path` MUST exist, and you must have read it in this conversation. To create a new file, use write instead.

`old_str` MUST exist in the file, matching it exactly, including whitespace and indentation. Leave out any line-number prefixes from read output.

`old_str` and `new_str` MUST be different from each other.

Set `replace_all` to true to replace all occurrences of `old_str` in the file. Else, `old_str` MUST be unique within the file or the edit will fail. Include more surrounding lines to make it unique.

If you need to replace the entire contents of a file, use write instead.

path.description: The absolute path to the file (MUST be absolute, not relative). File must exist.

old_str.description: Text to search for. Must match exactly.

replace_all.description: Set to true to replace all matches of old_str. Else, old_str must be an unique match. Defaults to false.

cw/amp@2/glob.description:
Find files whose paths match a glob pattern, in a codebase of any size.

Use this tool to find files by name patterns across the workspace. Results are sorted by most recent modification time first.

## When to use this tool

- When you need to find specific file types (for example all TypeScript files)
- When you want to find files in specific directories or following specific patterns
- When you need to explore the codebase structure quickly

## File pattern syntax

- `**/*.js` - all JavaScript files in any directory
- `src/**/*.ts` - all TypeScript files under the src directory
- `*.json` - all JSON files in the workspace root
- `**/*test*` - all files with "test" in the name
- `**/*.{js,ts}` - all JavaScript and TypeScript files

The search runs from the workspace root unless you give `path`. To search for text inside files, use grep instead.

filePattern.description: Glob pattern like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts" to match files

path.description: Optional absolute path of the directory to search from. Defaults to the workspace root.

cw/amp@2/grep.description:
Search file contents for a regular expression using ripgrep.

Returns the matching lines, each with its file path and line number.

## When to use this tool

- When you need to find text matches like variable names, function calls, or specific strings
- When you know the precise pattern you are looking for (including regex patterns)
- When you want to find all occurrences of a specific term across multiple files

## When not to use this tool

- To find files by name, use glob
- For a broad, conceptual question about how the code works, start a subagent with task

## Search pattern tips

- The pattern is a regular expression: escape special characters, for example `foo\(` to find calls of `foo`
- Use `glob` to limit the search to certain file types, for example `*.py` or `*.{ts,tsx}`
- Use `path` to search a single directory instead of the whole workspace
- Keep patterns specific; a very common word returns too many results to be useful

pattern.description: The regular expression to search for

path.description: Optional absolute path of the directory to search in. Defaults to the workspace root.

glob.description: Optional file glob to restrict which files are searched, e.g. "*.ts" or "*.{js,jsx}"

cw/amp@2/task.description:
Perform a task (a sub-task of the user's overall task) using a sub-agent that has access to the following tools: bash, read, write, edit, glob, grep.

When to use the task tool:
- When you need to perform complex multi-step work that can be described completely up front
- When you want to run independent pieces of work in parallel: start several sub-agents in one response, as long as they do not edit the same files
- When you need a careful second opinion: describe the job as "Review: ..." and tell the sub-agent to read and analyse only, never to change files

When NOT to use the task tool:
- When the job takes only a few tool calls you can make yourself
- When you need to see each intermediate step, or to react to what you find as you go
- When you are not yet sure what needs to be done

How to use the task tool:
- The sub-agent starts with no knowledge of this conversation. Put everything it needs in `prompt`: the goal, the relevant absolute paths, constraints, whether it may change files, and what to report back.
- `description` is a short label of three to six words shown in the session record.
- The sub-agent's final message is returned to you only; the user does not see it. Summarise anything relevant in your own response.
- Check the sub-agent's concrete claims and file changes before relying on them.
- This tool always starts a general sub-agent; any list of agent types shown below is for reference only and needs no argument from you.

prompt.description: The task for the sub-agent to perform. Be specific about what needs to be done and include any relevant context.

description.description: A very short description of the task, three to six words. Begin it with "Review:" for a read-only second opinion.

cw/augment@2/bash.description:
Launch a new process with a shell command and return its combined stdout and stderr as one text once it exits. There is no separate exit code field; append `; echo "exit=$?"` to the command when you need it. After a pipeline `$?` is the last command's status, so use `set -o pipefail;` first if an earlier stage matters.

- `command` (required): the shell command, run with bash.
- `cwd` (required): absolute path of the directory to run the command in.
- `max_wait_milliseconds` (optional): how long to wait before the process is killed, in milliseconds. If omitted, a default limit of 120000 ms (two minutes) applies. A killed command's result says that it timed out. Set it for slow builds, installs and test suites.

Notes:
- Each call is a fresh process; environment changes and `cd` do not carry over between calls.
- Commands must be non-interactive. For servers, start them in the background with output redirected to a file.
- Do not use this tool to read, search or edit files; `read`, `grep`, `glob` and `edit` do that better.
- Do not delete files you did not create unless the task asks for it.

cwd.description: Absolute path to the working directory for the command.

max_wait_milliseconds.description: Optional. Maximum number of milliseconds to wait for the command to finish (default 120000).

cw/augment@2/read.description:
Read a file or list a directory.

- `path` (required): path of the file or directory, absolute or relative to the working directory.
- `view_start_line` (optional): 1-based line number to start reading at.
- `view_line_count` (optional): number of lines to return.

For a file, the output gives `<path>`, `<type>` and then `<content>`, where each line looks like `12: text` (line number, colon, the line); use these numbers for `old_str_start_line_number_1` and `old_str_end_line_number_1` in `edit`. For a directory, the output lists its entries. Without `view_line_count` at most 2000 lines are shown, followed by a hint naming the `view_start_line` value to continue from; read long files in windows with `view_start_line` and `view_line_count`. Binary files are better inspected with `head -c`, `od` or `strings` through `bash`. Prefer reading the whole relevant region in one call over many tiny calls.

path.description: Path to the file or directory.

view_line_count.description: Optional number of lines to show.

cw/augment@2/write.description:
Save a new file. Use this tool only to create files that do not exist yet; for changes to an existing file use `edit` instead. Parent directories are created automatically. If the path already exists, the tool refuses unless you have opened the file with `read` in this session and it has not changed on disk since, and even then use `edit` instead.

- `path` (required): path of the file to create.
- `file_content` (required): the complete content of the file.
- `instructions_reminder` (required): always the text "LIMIT THE FILE CONTENT TO AT MOST 300 LINES. IF MORE CONTENT NEEDS TO BE ADDED USE THE edit TOOL TO EDIT THE FILE AFTER IT HAS BEEN CREATED."

Keep new files to about 300 lines; create the first part and extend it with `edit`.

instructions_reminder.description: Should be exactly this string: 'LIMIT THE FILE CONTENT TO AT MOST 300 LINES. IF MORE CONTENT NEEDS TO BE ADDED USE THE edit TOOL TO EDIT THE FILE AFTER IT HAS BEEN CREATED.'

cw/augment@2/edit.description:
Edit an existing file by replacing one exact string. This is the only tool for changing existing files; do not rewrite them with `write` or with shell commands.

Arguments:
- `instruction_reminder` (required): always the text "ALWAYS BREAK DOWN EDITS INTO SMALLER CHUNKS OF AT MOST 150 LINES EACH."
- `path` (required): path of the file to edit.
- `old_str_1` (required): the exact text to replace. It must match the file exactly, whitespace included, and must occur exactly once. Add surrounding lines if needed to make it unique.
- `new_str_1` (required): the replacement text. It may be empty to delete `old_str_1`.
- `old_str_start_line_number_1` (optional): 1-based line number of the first line of `old_str_1` in the file.
- `old_str_end_line_number_1` (optional): 1-based line number of the last line of `old_str_1` in the file (inclusive).

Notes:
- This tool applies one replacement per call; the `_1` suffix names the single edit set. For several changes, make several calls.
- Give the two optional line number hints whenever you have a recent `read` of the region. They document which occurrence you mean but are not checked; the match itself is decided by `old_str_1` alone.
- The tool refuses to edit a file you have not opened with `read` in this session, or one that changed on disk since that read; read it (again) first. After an edit, line numbers below the edited region may shift.
- Keep `old_str_1` and `new_str_1` under about 150 lines each.

instruction_reminder.description: Reminder to limit edits to at most 150 lines. Should be exactly this string: 'ALWAYS BREAK DOWN EDITS INTO SMALLER CHUNKS OF AT MOST 150 LINES EACH.'

path.description: Path of the file to edit.

old_str_1.description: Exact string in the file to replace.

old_str_start_line_number_1.description: Optional. 1-based line number of the first line of old_str_1.

old_str_end_line_number_1.description: Optional. 1-based line number of the last line of old_str_1, inclusive.

cw/augment@2/glob.description:
Find files whose path matches a glob pattern, such as "**/*.ts" or "tests/**/test_*.py". Returns matching paths, most recently modified first.

- `glob_pattern` (required): the pattern to match.
- `path` (optional): directory to search in; defaults to the working directory.

Patterns are relative to `path`: a bare pattern such as "*.py" matches only that directory's own files, so start it with "**/" to search at any depth. Use it to locate files by name before reading them. Keep patterns specific in large projects.

glob_pattern.description: Glob pattern to match file paths against.

path.description: Optional directory to search in.

cw/augment@2/grep.description:

Use it to find definitions, call sites, error messages and configuration keys before you edit anything. Search for every symbol you plan to change.

path.description: Optional directory to search in.

file_glob.description: Optional glob that file names must match.

cw/bank-compliance@2/bash.description:
Runs one shell command line in the sandbox and returns its standard output and standard error together, as one block of text. There is no separate exit-status field; when the status matters, append something like `; echo "exit=$?"` to the `shell_command`. After a pipe, `$?` is the last command's status: use `set -o pipefail` or save the status first.

Control notes (ENG-AI-STD-014 Part 5):
- Every call starts a new shell. Use `run_directory` instead of a leading cd; chain dependent steps with && in one `shell_command`.
- Commands must be non-interactive. Pass -y / --yes style flags and set PAGER=cat where a program may page.
- Start servers in the background with output redirected to a log file in the temporary directory, then check them with a second call.
- `timeout_ms` defaults to about 120000 (two minutes). Raise it for builds, installs and long test runs.
- Keep output short (tail, head, grep); long output is cut.
- Do not use this tool to read or change files that `read`, `edit` or `write` can handle; bounded inspection of binary or very large files (head -c, od, strings) is allowed.
- Do not depend on outside network. Version-control history must not be changed (CM-7). The sandbox refuses `rm -rf` on absolute paths, git fetch/pull/clone, `git log --all` and `git reflog`; clean up with relative paths.

Runs a bash command in the working directory and returns its stdout and stderr together as one text, with an optional timeout. Each call starts a fresh shell: a `cd` or an exported variable does not carry over to the next call.

Before you run a command, go through these steps:

1. Check the target location:
   - If the command creates files or folders, confirm first (for example with `ls -d` on the parent) that the parent exists and is the place you mean.
   - For example, before `mkdir build/out`, make sure `build` is there.

2. Run the command:
   - Put double quotes around any path that contains spaces.
   - Quoting examples:
     - python "/srv/data files/convert.py" (correct)
     - python /srv/data files/convert.py (wrong: the shell splits the path in two)
   - With the quoting right, run the command and read its output.

Usage notes:
  - `command` is required.
  - `description` is required too: five to ten words in the active voice saying what the command does. For `ls -la` write "List files in current directory"; for `npm install`, "Install package dependencies"; for `pytest -x tests/test_api.py`, "Run API tests and stop at first failure".
  - `timeout` is optional, in milliseconds, at most 600000 (10 minutes). Without it a command is stopped after 120000 ms (2 minutes); a stopped command's result says it was killed.
  - Long output is cut before it reaches you. Narrow the command (pipe through grep, head or tail) when you need only part of it.
  - For work that outlasts the timeout, start it in the background with its output going to a log file (for example `nohup ./long_job.sh > job.log 2>&1 &`) and look at the log in later calls.
  - VERY IMPORTANT: for text files, do not explore with shell commands such as `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail` or `ls -R`. The glob, grep and read tools do that job better. Binary or very large files (executables, archives, multi-megabyte data files) are the exception: inspect them here with `head -c`, `od`, `strings` or `objdump`. If you really need a text search inside a pipeline, prefer `rg` when it is installed.
  - The sandbox refuses `rm -rf` on absolute paths (use relative ones, such as `rm -rf build/`) and git network or history-mining commands (`git fetch`, `git pull`, `git clone`, `git log --all`, `git reflog`).
  - Nothing can type into a running command, so never start editors, pagers, interactive prompts, `git rebase -i` or `git add -i`. Use the non-interactive flags instead.
  - Separate several commands with ';' or '&&', not with newlines (newlines are fine inside quoted strings).
  - Use absolute paths rather than `cd`, so every call is clear about where it runs. Use `cd` only when a tool insists on being run from a particular folder, and then in the same command.
    <good-example>
    pytest /path/to/project/tests
    </good-example>
    <bad-example>
    cd /path/to/project && pytest tests
    </bad-example>

# Git

Commit only when the user explicitly asks for a commit. Leave the git configuration alone, avoid destructive commands (hard resets, forced checkouts, clean, history rewrites) unless that exact operation was requested, never skip hooks, and never push: there is no remote to publish to. Before a requested commit, look at `git status`, `git diff` and recent `git log`, stage files by name, and pass the message through a heredoc.

cw/enterprise-assistant@1/bash.description:

cw/enterprise-assistant@1/read.description:

cw/enterprise-assistant@1/grep.description:

cw/gemini-cli@2/bash.description:
Runs one shell command with bash and returns what it printed. Each call gets a fresh shell, so a `cd` or an exported variable is gone by the next call; use `dir_path` to pick the directory instead. A trailing `&` starts a background process.

cw/gemini-cli@2/read.description: Returns one file's text: the result shows the path and type, then the content with each line written as `N: text`, where N is the 1-based line number (not part of the file). Without `limit` it shows up to 2000 lines; when more remain it ends with a hint naming the `offset` to continue from. Binary files are refused; inspect those, or very large files, with `head -c`, `od` or `strings` through `bash`. Pointing `absolute_path` at a directory lists its entries instead, which is how you list a directory.

cw/gemini-cli@2/edit.description:

- `old_string` is literal text and may not be empty, not a regex and not escaped, and must match the file exactly, whitespace and indentation included.
- Without `allow_multiple`, `old_string` must occur exactly once; if it occurs several times the edit fails. Give it enough surrounding lines (two or three above and below the change usually suffice) to make it unique.
- With `allow_multiple` set to true, every occurrence is replaced, so a short string such as a name is fine.
- `instruction` says in plain words what the change is for. It is kept as a record and does not affect the edit.

To create a new file, use `write`.

cw/gemini-cli@2/glob.description: Lists files whose path matches a glob pattern such as `**/*.py` or `src/**/*.ts`. cw/gemini-cli@2/task.description:

cw/gemini-cli@2/todowrite.description:
Keeps the task list for the current request: the steps still to do, the one in hand and the ones finished. It helps you stay organised on longer work and not drop a step.

Each call replaces the whole list. Every item in `todos` has `content` (the step), `status` and `priority`.

1. pending: not started yet.
2. in_progress: being worked on now. Keep exactly one item in this state.
3. completed: done, with nothing left blocking it.
4. cancelled: dropped because the work turned out not to need it.

Priority is one of high, medium, low.

How to use it:
1. Use it when the request takes several steps; skip it for one or two quick steps.
2. Write the list once the steps are clear, and rewrite it when the plan changes.
3. Set an item to in_progress right before starting it and to completed right after finishing it.

cw/goose@2/bash.description: Run a single shell command and get its combined stdout and stderr back. cw/ide-agent@2/bash.description:

cw/windsurf@2/edit.description:
Use this tool to edit an existing file by replacing one exact block of text. The call FAILS on a file you have not viewed with read in this session.

Notes:
- `TargetFile` is the absolute path of the file to modify. Specify it first.
- `Instruction` is required: one sentence describing what this change does and why.
- `ReplacementChunk` holds the change: `TargetContent` is the exact text currently in the file, including whitespace and indentation, and `ReplacementContent` is the text that replaces it. The two must differ.
- The edit FAILS if `TargetContent` is not found, or if it is found more than once and `AllowMultiple` is not true. Add neighbouring lines to make it unique. Set `AllowMultiple` to true only to replace every occurrence.
- Never include line-number prefixes from the view output in `TargetContent` or `ReplacementContent`.
- `CodeMarkdownLanguage` is optional: the language of the file (for example python, typescript, bash), recorded with the change.
- For several separate changes in one file, make several calls.

toolSummary.description: A short phrase (two to six words) summarizing what this call does, for example "checking test fixtures". Give it first.

TargetFile.description: The absolute path of the file to modify.

Instruction.description: One sentence describing what this change does and why.

CodeMarkdownLanguage.description: Optional language name of the file, such as python or go.

ReplacementChunk.description: The block of text to replace and its replacement.

TargetContent.description: The exact text to replace. Must be unique in the file unless AllowMultiple is true.

AllowMultiple.description: Optional. If true, replace every occurrence of TargetContent. Defaults to false.

cw/windsurf@2/glob.description:
Find files by name with a glob pattern. Returns matching file paths, most recently modified first.

Notes:
- `Pattern` is the glob to match, for example **/*.go or src/**/test_*.py. It is relative to `SearchDirectory`; a pattern such as *.go without **/ matches only files directly inside that directory.
- `SearchDirectory` is the absolute path of the directory to search in. Optional; defaults to the workspace.
- Use this tool, not shell find or ls, to locate files by name. Run several searches in parallel when you have several guesses.
- `toolSummary` is optional.

toolSummary.description: A short phrase (two to six words) summarizing what this call does, for example "checking test fixtures". Give it first.

Pattern.description: The glob pattern to match file paths against.

SearchDirectory.description: Optional absolute path of the directory to search. Defaults to the workspace.

cw/windsurf@2/grep.description:
Search file contents with a regular expression. Returns the files that contain a match, with the matching lines and their line numbers.

Notes:
- `Query` is the regular expression to search for (for example def parse_\w+ or "TODO|FIXME"). Escape regex special characters when you mean them literally.
- `SearchPath` is the absolute path of the directory or file to search. Optional; defaults to the workspace.
- `Includes` is an optional glob that limits which files are searched, for example *.py or *.{ts,tsx}.
- Use this tool, not shell grep or rg, for searching code. Results may be capped; narrow the query or the path if you get too many.
- `toolSummary` is optional.

toolSummary.description: A short phrase (two to six words) summarizing what this call does, for example "checking test fixtures". Give it first.

Query.description: The regular expression to search for.

SearchPath.description: Optional absolute path of the directory or file to search. Defaults to the workspace.

Includes.description: Optional glob pattern for the files to search, such as *.js.

cw/xml-synthetic@2/bash.description: Run a single shell command in a fresh bash shell started in the working directory, and return stdout and stderr combined as one text. There is no exit code field: append ; echo "exit=$?" when the status matters (after a pipeline that is the last command's status unless set -o pipefail is on). Every call must include `reason`, one short sentence saying why the command is run. `timeout` is optional, in milliseconds; give long builds and test suites a generous one. Join dependent steps with && inside one `command`. Filter large outputs with head, tail or grep. Do not depend on network access.

reason.description: One short sentence: why this command is run.

cw/xml-synthetic@2/read.description: Read a file and return its lines with line numbers, or list the entries of a directory. `location.file` is required. `location.start_line` (1-based) and `location.max_lines` are optional; use them to page through large files. Lines come back as `N: text`; the prefix is not part of the file text. Without `max_lines` up to 2000 lines are shown; if the result ends with "Use location.start_line=N to continue", call again with `location.start_line` set to N. Example: {"location": {"file": "src/app.py", "start_line": 120, "max_lines": 60}}.

file.description: Path of the file or directory to read.

max_lines.description: Optional number of lines to return.

cw/xml-synthetic@2/write.description: Write `content` as the whole content of the file at `location.file`, replacing it if it exists and creating parent folders if needed. Both arguments are required. Read an existing file before you replace it. Use `edit` instead for small changes to existing files.

file.description: Path of the file, relative to the working directory or absolute.

cw/xml-synthetic@2/edit.description: Replace text in an existing file. The call fails if the file was not read in this session or changed on disk since. `location.file` names the file. `change.before` is the exact current text and must occur exactly once, unless `change.every` is true, in which case every occurrence is replaced. `change.after` is the new text. Copy `change.before` from a recent `read` of the file, keeping whitespace exactly and leaving out line numbers. Example: {"location": {"file": "src/app.py"}, "change": {"before": "x = 1", "after": "x = 2"}}. `change` is an object, not a string.

file.description: Path of the file, relative to the working directory or absolute.

after.description: Text to put in its place.

every.description: Optional. Replace every occurrence of `before` (default false).

cw/xml-synthetic@2/glob.description: Find files whose paths match a glob `pattern` such as `**/*.ts` or `src/**/test_*.py`. `under` is an optional folder to search in; it defaults to the working directory. Patterns are relative to `under`; a pattern without `**/` (such as `*.ts`) matches only directly inside that folder. Returns matching paths.

cw/xml-synthetic@2/grep.description: Search file contents for a regular expression `pattern`. `under` is an optional folder (defaults to the working directory); `files` is an optional file-name filter such as `*.py` or `*.{c,h}`. Returns matching files with line numbers.

cw/zed@3/bash.description:
Runs a one-line shell command in a bash shell and returns its combined standard output and standard error as one text. No separate exit status is returned; read the output to tell success from failure.

The command runs in the directory given by `cd`, which every call must include (a call without it is rejected). Do not include shell substitutions or interpolations such as `$VAR`, `${VAR}`, `$(...)`, backticks or `$((...))`; resolve those values first and write the literal value. For logic that needs variables or several lines, write a script file with `write` and run it.

REMINDER: read-only git commands (`git log`, `git diff`, `git blame`; the sandbox refuses `git show` and `git cat-file`) MUST include `--no-pager` (for example `git --no-pager log`). Prefer `git --no-optional-locks status`. Git commands that may open an editor (`git rebase`, `git commit`, `git merge`, `git tag`) MUST start with `GIT_EDITOR=true `, or the terminal will hang.

Use `timeout_ms` for builds, test suites and anything that may run for a long time. Do not use this tool to read, write or search files when `read`, `write`, `edit`, `glob` or `grep` can do it.

cd.description: Required on every call. Working directory for the command, as an absolute path: normally the project root or a directory inside it.

timeout_ms.description: Optional maximum runtime in milliseconds. If it is exceeded, the command is killed and the result says so.

cw/zed@3/read.description:
Reads the content of a file in the project, with line numbers. For a directory, lists its entries instead.

For large files, pass `start_line` and `line_count` to read only the part you need. Without them the tool returns up to 2000 lines from the start, each as `N: text`, and says which `start_line` continues. For binary or very large files, `bash` with `head -c`, `od` or `strings` may suit better.

path.description: Absolute path of the file or directory, for example `{{cwd}}/src/main.rs`. Project files start with the project root; use another absolute path only when the task names it or for scratch files under `/tmp`. Do not guess paths; find them with `glob` or `grep` first.

start_line.description: Optional line number to start reading on (1-based).

line_count.description: Optional number of lines to read, starting at start_line.

cw/zed@3/write.description:
Creates a new file, or overwrites an existing one, with the given content. Parent directories are created as needed.

Use it for new files and for full rewrites of small files. To change part of an existing file, use `edit` instead. Overwriting an existing file is refused unless you have opened it with `read` in this session and it has not changed since; a new file needs no read. `display_description` is required and only labels the change.

display_description.description: A one-line, human-readable summary of this change, shown in the list of edits (for example "Add retry to fetch_config"). Keep it under about ten words. It does not affect the file.

path.description: Absolute path of the file, for example `{{cwd}}/src/main.rs`. Project files start with the project root; use another absolute path only when the task names it or for scratch files under `/tmp`. Do not guess paths; find them with `glob` or `grep` first.

content.description: The entire content for the file.

cw/zed@3/edit.description:
Edits a file by finding `old_text` and replacing it with `new_text`.

- Read the file with `read` first. The edit is refused if you have not read this file in this session, or if it changed on disk since you read it; do not edit from memory.
- `old_text` must match the file exactly, including whitespace and indentation, and must appear exactly once. If it matches more than once, include more surrounding lines so it is unique, or set `replace_all` to true to change every occurrence.
- `new_text` should keep the file's indentation and style.
- One call makes one replacement (or every occurrence with `replace_all`). For several separate changes in a file, make several calls.
- `display_description` is required and only labels the change; it does not affect the file.

display_description.description: A one-line, human-readable summary of this change, shown in the list of edits (for example "Add retry to fetch_config"). Keep it under about ten words. It does not affect the file.

path.description: Absolute path of the file, for example `{{cwd}}/src/main.rs`. Project files start with the project root; use another absolute path only when the task names it or for scratch files under `/tmp`. Do not guess paths; find them with `glob` or `grep` first.

old_text.description: The exact text to find in the file. It must match once unless replace_all is true.

replace_all.description: Optional. Replace every occurrence of old_text instead of exactly one. Defaults to false.

cw/zed@3/glob.description:
Finds files in the project whose paths match a glob pattern, searching from the project root. Returns matching paths, most recently modified first.

It cannot search outside the project root; use `bash` with `find` for that. Use it when you know part of a file name but not its full path. For example, a `glob` of `**/*config*.toml` finds every TOML file with "config" in its name.

glob.description: The glob to match against file paths in the project, for example `**/*.rs` or `src/**/test_*.py`.

cw/zed@3/grep.description:
Searches the contents of files in the project for a regular expression and returns each matching line with its file path and line number.

Use it to find symbols, strings and error messages. Do NOT put a path in `regex`; it is matched only against file contents. To restrict the search to certain files, set `include_pattern`. As you learn the layout of the project, narrow your searches instead of searching everything again.

regex.description: A regular expression to search for in file contents.

include_pattern.description: Optional glob for the files to include, for example `*.rs` or `*.{ts,tsx}`. If omitted, all files are searched.

cw/zed@3/task.description:
Starts a sub-agent with its own fresh context and the same file and terminal tools, and returns its final message.

The sub-agent cannot see this conversation, so `message` must contain everything it needs: the goal, relevant paths, constraints and what to report back. `label` is a short name for the job. Use it for large, separable work or independent investigations, not for lookups you can do in one or two calls. The kind of sub-agent is chosen for you; ignore any list of agent types that may follow this description.

label.description: Short label for the sub-agent's job, for example "Survey test setup".

message.description: The full, self-contained instructions for the sub-agent.
